props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a compact 2D Godot platformer - read the landing, commit to one fixed-height jump, die fast, retry instantly - into a playable Godot project. Keep the starter's tuning untouched. Replace the character's visual identity. Extend the real level so the flag can only be reached through the new section. Measure every jump rather than trusting the arithmetic.

beats.role_note: What was actually built, with one meaningful correction. States the slice's limits, not the full GDD's promises.
beats.narration_text: The name fools you. This is not the three-zone course the design document proposes. It is one level slice: the starter's two gaps and one spike cluster, plus a new tower where the floor stops existing. Four new landings, a spike gate, and a flag you have to climb to. And the correction worth making early - the brief promised two converging routes so the player could choose a risk level. That turned out to be geometrically impossible. This film shows why, and what replaced it.

beats.role_note: Cause and effect number one, from VERBATIM project source. Why the starter's death showed nothing and this one shows something.
beats.narration_text: Why did that death look like anything? In the starter it did not. Killing the player sets enabled to false, and the player's physics function returns on its first line while disabled - so it stops asking to be redrawn and freezes on whatever frame it died on. The starter printed the words and changed nothing. The fix is six lines in the session: advance a counter, ask the player to redraw, ask the level to redraw. No timing, no physics, no collision value moves. The retry window is still the same zero point five five seconds, and the mechanics suite still reports a maximum of thirty-four ticks, bit-identical to the unmodified starter.

beats.role_note: The measurement that built the level, and the honest failure it exposed. Numbers are from evidence/reach-*.json.
beats.narration_text: None of those landings were placed by arithmetic. A headless harness drops the real player at a take-off position, two pixels at a time, jumps, and records where it actually ends up. It reads nothing from the tuning resource, so a level that only passes because the jump got stronger cannot pass it. The windows came back between fifty-four and eighty-six pixels, and zero of forty ground take-offs crossed the chasm - which is what makes the tower mandatory rather than scenery. The same measurement killed the brief's two-route plan. A twenty-eight pixel player standing on a sixteen pixel platform needs fifty-six pixels of separation before a second lane can exist above it. The measured peak rise is fifty-three point three. No lower lane can ever reach an upper one, so the geometry changed instead of the tuning.

props.heading: The harness reads no tuning value.
props.body:
verify_reach.gd sweeps the real player's take-off x in 2 px steps and records where it lands.
Measured windows: 54–86 px across nine jumps, including the two unchanged starter gaps.
Gate: 0 of 40 ground-level take-offs reach the far side of the chasm — the tower is mandatory.
Fork ruled out: 28 px player + 16 px platform needs 56 px of lane separation; peak rise is 53.3 px.
props.verdictLabel: Gets right: geometry changed, tuning did not.
props.sparkLine: Fifty-three point three is the ceiling.

beats.role_note: Cause and effect number two, from VERBATIM starter source. Why those summit spikes would have been drawn in the wrong place.
beats.narration_text: Those spikes on the summit are the second cause and effect, and this is the code that would have got them wrong. This is the starter's, verbatim. It walks the hazard list and draws each triangle between two literal numbers: three hundred and twenty for the base, three hundred and four for the point. Both are the old ground line. The trigger polygons are built from each hazard's own rectangle, so moving a hazard up onto a platform moves what kills you and leaves the picture behind. The summit gate sits at one hundred and eighty-four. Under this code it would have been painted a hundred and thirty-six pixels lower, on the ground, while the thing that kills you waited invisibly on the platform. That is the exact failure the assignment warns about. Drawing now reads each hazard's own top and height, and mirrors the trigger builder parameter for parameter.

beats.role_note: Separates observed working features from defects, untested claims and planned work.
beats.narration_text: The verdict. Working and shown: the new identity, four new landings, a chasm that gates the flag, both death conditions, pause, manual restart, completion and replay. Measured rather than asserted: every take-off window, and the fact that no ground take-off crosses the chasm. Honest failures: the two-route fork cannot exist at this tuning, and the berries were added to supply that missing choice and do not. Eighty-three to one hundred percent of every safe window collects them anyway, because the player is a body sweeping a parabola, not a point tracing one. Still open: the camera is static for the last three hundred pixels of the climb, it never pans vertically, and exactly one person has played this. A scripted route is not a playtest.

beats.role_note: Your Turn - a paste-ready Walker prompt and one concrete experiment. Liam signs off here, before the final card.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the paste-ready prompt. Take a Godot starter and, before you place a single platform, derive from its tuning what a jump actually gives you: peak rise, airtime, and the landing window for a given rise. Then write a harness that sweeps the real player across those windows and tells you the truth. The concrete experiment: add one optional route a competent player can skip, and measure what share of the safe window takes it anyway. If that number comes back near one hundred percent, you built decoration, not a decision - and you will know it before you write the narration instead of after. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Read this Godot project's tuning resource and derive, before designing anything: peak rise, airtime, flat jump distance, and the landing window for a rise of R. Then write a headless harness that sweeps the real player's take-off position in 2 px steps and reports, per jump, the window that actually lands. Build the level from those measurements. Do not raise jump strength to make geometry fit — change the geometry. Finally, add one optional pickup and measure what share of each safe take-off window collects it anyway.
props.runningText: deriving reach from tuning.gd; sweeping the real player…
output: if a route needs more rise than the tuning gives, the route is wrong — not the tuning
a pickup collected by 83–100% of safe take-offs is decoration; a decision has to cost something
distrust the flattering measurement: this project's first cherry sweep read 0–4% and was broken
